title: Passwords that hold + 2FA that helps
body: A password manager plus a second factor beats memorized cleverness. Pick one manager, turn on app-based 2FA for email first, then bank and school accounts. Write down backup codes on paper. Quiz and flashcards only in Recruit — no terminal in this band by design.

quiz.q: Your email offers SMS codes or an authenticator app. Which holds up better against SIM-swap theft?
What does the CIA triad's 'Confidentiality' mean here?
choices: Only the right people can read it

title: Spot phishing without clicking
body: Check the sender address letter by letter, hover links instead of tapping, and treat urgency plus attachments as a stop sign. Real schools don't ask for passwords over chat. When unsure, open the official site yourself instead of following the message link.

quiz.q: A message says 'account locked, verify now' with a short link. Safest move?
choices: Type the official site address yourself
Reply with your ID to confirm

title: CIA triad, malware names, encryption in plain words
body: Confidentiality, Integrity, Availability. Viruses need a host file, worms move on their own, trojans pretend to be useful, ransomware locks files for payment. Encryption scrambles readable text with a key; hashing is one-way fingerprinting. Knowing the names keeps later lessons readable.

quiz.q: Ransomware primarily breaks which leg of the triad?
Hashing a password is best described as?

title: Recruit checkpoint
body: Gate before Operator. Pass at 70% to unlock the terminal band. No terminal questions here — that starts at level 11.

quiz.q: Someone calls claiming to be IT and asks for your one-time code. You?
choices: Read it out, they sound senior
Refuse and report via official channel
Ask them to text from personal number
Save passwords in browser on shared PC

title: OSI and TCP/IP without tears
body: Seven OSI layers, four TCP/IP layers — but you only need the working map: Link gets frames to neighbors, Internet (IP) routes packets, Transport (TCP/UDP) orders or fires, Application (HTTP/DNS/SSH) talks. When a lab says '80/tcp open', read it as: IP reachable, TCP handshake worked, something answers HTTP. Twice the depth of Recruit: names plus reading outputs.

quiz.q: TCP vs UDP in one line?
choices: TCP orders and retries, UDP fires and forgets

quiz.q: An IP address lives at which layer?

title: Linux: ls, cd, cat without fear
body: First terminal band. Open the linux-basics lab: pwd, ls, ls -la, cat readme.txt, cat /home/recruit/flag.txt. Guided and fully scripted — every command has one right place to run. Everything here runs against a fake machine we ship.

quiz.q: Which command lists files including hidden ones?
Which command prints a text file?

title: Ports and protocols you will actually meet
body: Common doors: 22 SSH, 53 DNS, 80 HTTP, 443 HTTPS, 3306 MySQL. The scan-sim lab pretends to knock on these so you learn reading output, not touching real hosts. Pair with the OSI lesson: port numbers belong to Transport, service names to Application.

title: Permissions and tiny scripts
body: rwx for user, group, other. chmod +x makes a script runnable. A three-line bash loop beats clicking 50 times; a five-line Python loop beats bash for text. The lab asks you to read one permission string and run one safe local script — still inside our sandbox.

choices: Repeating a safe check many times

title: Operator checkpoint + terminal gate
body: Pass this plus the linux-basics lab flag to reach Analyst. From here hints cost coins and hand-holding drops.

title: OSINT without stalking
body: Practice on fictional 'Alon Freight'. Check the fake site map, staff page, and DNS-style records in the lab. Collect what's public, write source + date per fact, stop before contact or intrusion. Real people and real companies are off limits — this habit is what separates analysts from stalkers.

choices: Messaging an employee to trick them
Listing public subdomains of the practice target

title: Enumeration and reading scan output
body: Enumeration turns one address into a list: hostnames, ports, services, versions. The scan-sim lab fakes an nmap-style table — your job is reading, not running: which ports are open, what service that suggests, what to probe next. Hints here cost 1.5x Operator prices because the answers are longer.

quiz.q: Next step after finding 80/tcp open on the practice box?
choices: Probe the web app we ship
Try default passwords on real routers

title: SQL injection and XSS, safely demoed
body: A login form that builds SQL by gluing strings breaks on ' OR '1'='1. A comment box echoing raw HTML lets scripts run. Our practice app shows both with a reset button, plus the fix side: parameterized queries, output escaping, CSP. Never test this on real sites — lab only.

choices: Saved then shown to others without escaping

title: CSRF and the practice app
body: Cross-Site Request Forgery rides your logged-in session: a malicious page triggers an action you didn't mean. Defense is SameSite cookies, anti-CSRF tokens, and checking intent on state-changing requests. The practice app demos a forged 'change email' request and its token fix. Roughly double the Operator depth: now you chain request, session, and defense.

choices: Your live session on another site

title: Analyst checkpoint
body: Gate to Specialist. Requires the scan-sim flag plus this quiz. Specialist is where PBQ-style recall stops being enough — multi-step boxes start.

quiz.q: Simulated scan shows 80/tcp open. That usually means?
choices: A web server may be there

title: Privilege escalation, concept-first
body: Getting a foothold is step one; misconfigurations decide step two: world-writable scripts, stray sudo rules, weak service permissions. The privesc-sim lab gives a fake sudo -l readout and three files — you read, pick the intended path, and submit the flag. No real systems, no kernel exploits, just the habit of checking config before cleverness.

quiz.q: First privesc check on a Linux box?

title: Hashes, salts, and wordlists
body: MD5/SHA are fast fingerprints, bcrypt/argon2 are slow on purpose. Salts stop rainbow tables; pepper and cost factors slow brute force. The hash-drill lab hands a known MD5 plus a 4-word list — crack it, then answer why the same trick fails on salted bcrypt. Double Analyst depth: mechanism plus why the easy path dies.

title: Stack overflows, safely caged
body: A fixed-size buffer plus unchecked input overwrites the return address — that is the whole bug in one sentence. The bof-sim lab runs a fake vulnerable program: feed it lengths, watch the offset report, find EIP control without any shellcode, then answer how canaries, ASLR, and NX break the real version. Concept + mitigation, no weaponized payload.

choices: Adjacent stack data, possibly the return address

title: Active Directory paths, mapped not run
body: AD attacks are graph problems: users → groups → privileges → Domain Admin. Kerberoasting, AS-REP roasting, and token theft abuse real protocol edges. Our lesson is map-reading on a drawn fictional domain — find the shortest path, name the fix (strong passwords, no pre-auth disabled, tiered admins). You never touch a real domain here.

quiz.q: AD attack paths are best seen as?

title: Wireless basics, hands off neighbors
body: WPA2/WPA3 handshakes, evil twins, and why open cafe Wi-Fi plus no VPN leaks. No capturing, no deauth — the lesson is reading a sanitized handshake diagram and picking defenses: WPA3, strong PSK, VPN on open nets, forgetting hostile SSIDs. Touching neighbor networks stays out of bounds everywhere on this site.

choices: VPN + HTTPS, forget the net after
A fake AP copying a legit name

title: Specialist checkpoint
body: Gate to Red Team. Quiz gate at 70% plus XP; bring hash-drill and privesc-sim flags as proof of practice. This is the wall PBQ-only study can't climb — multi-step chaining starts next.

quiz.q: AD fix that kills many paths?

title: Chained attacks, MITRE-style
body: Real intrusions chain: recon → initial access → execution → persistence → privilege escalation → defense evasion → collection → exfiltration. Map each lab step you already did onto ATT&CK tactics, then plan a fictional 4-stage chain in the worksheet. Double Specialist depth: single boxes become campaigns with detection points at every hop.

choices: Recon, access, execution, persistence, collection, exfil
One missed hop still catches the chain

title: SSRF and deserialization, caged
body: SSRF tricks a server into fetching internal URLs; unsafe deserialization turns crafted data into code. The ssrf-sim lab gives a fake fetcher with an allowlist off by one character — find the bypass path, read the metadata-style file, submit the flag, then write the fix (allowlist, no internal fetches, signed serializers). Fictional fetcher only.

choices: Trusted schemas, signed data, no eval

title: Malware analysis without malware
body: Static first (strings, headers, hashes), dynamic second (sandboxed API calls, network), never on your daily machine. Our lesson uses printed fake reports — list persistence tricks, C2 signs, and why you hash before uploading anywhere. No live samples ship or needed.

choices: Hashes/strings first, sandbox second, bare metal never

title: Cloud misconfigs vs fake AWS
body: Public S3-style buckets, wide-open security groups, leaked keys in fake repos. The cloud-sim lab lists buckets and policies — find the world-readable one, quote the policy line, submit the flag, then write the fix (least privilege, block-public defaults, key rotation). Fake cloud only; real account IDs never appear.

title: Red Team checkpoint
body: Gate to Apex. Quiz gate at 70% plus XP; ssrf-sim and cloud-sim flags are the matching hands-on proof. Apex mixes offense with defense under a timer.

title: Blue team: logs and incident response
body: Offense halves the picture. Read the logs-sim bundle: auth failures, odd hours, new processes, outbound spikes. Triage with PICERL (prepare, identify, contain, eradicate, recover, lessons), write a one-paragraph incident note, and name what you'd alert vs ignore. Timed in the boss mission — calm reading beats fast clicking.

quiz.q: First IR move on suspected compromise?

title: Boss battle: everything chained
body: Timed capstone mixing every band: hygiene call, Linux find, scan read, web bug, hash crack, cloud policy, log triage — seven flags, one clock, hints locked to tier-1 only. Pass here and Prestige unlocks: reset to level 1 with a permanent badge plus the monthly rotator pool.

choices: Breadth first, hardest flag last, notes always
Reset to 1 with badge + harder monthly pool

title: Apex checkpoint
body: Final gate. Quiz at 70% plus XP; soc-logs-ir and boss-battle work is the matching proof. Clears the Prestige button on your profile.

choices: Chained offense + calm defense under time

title: Monthly rotator (prestige pool)
body: Harder monthly set for prestiged players: re-rolled flags, tighter timers, tier-1 hints only. Same fictional boxes, meaner configs. New prompt lands the first of each month — this prototype ships January's set so the loop is visible.

choices: New flags, tighter time, minimal hints
